result:
The first thing the sea returned was a yellow glove.

It lay on the harbor steps with its fingers full of sand. Mara found it while unlocking the ferry office, shook it out, and hung it on the railing. By noon, three people had recognized it.

“My father’s,” said the baker.

“My daughter’s,” said a woman waiting for the mainland boat.

“Mine,” said a boy who had never owned gloves.

Mara left it where it was.

The next morning there was a teaspoon, a bicycle bell, and a photograph of a woman standing beside a horse. The woman’s face had washed away. The horse looked remarkably pleased with itself.

By Friday, the harbor steps were crowded.

Not with treasure. There were no gold coins, no jeweled swords, none of the things the council chairman mentioned when he called the newspaper. Instead, the sea delivered spectacles, hair clips, a cracked casserole dish, fourteen keys, and a wooden ruler bearing the name of a school that had burned down thirty years earlier.

People came carrying shopping bags.

They bent over the objects with the embarrassed concentration of adults searching for something beneath a restaurant table.

Occasionally someone cried.

Mostly they said, “Well, would you look at that.”

Mara kept the ferry running.

She sold tickets through the little window and told passengers that yes, the afternoon crossing was still scheduled, and no, the objects were not included in the fare. When the newspaper reporter asked what she thought was happening, she said the sea was clearing a cupboard.

He printed that beneath a photograph of someone else.

On the ninth day, it returned a door.

Blue paint. Brass handle. Three shallow scratches near the bottom.

Mara knew it before she reached the steps.

Her father had painted that door every other summer, choosing the same blue from the same shop and then complaining that they had changed the mixture. The scratches were from a dog they had owned for six months. The dog had run away during a thunderstorm. For years afterward, her father stepped outside whenever he heard barking.

The house itself was gone.

Not taken by the sea. Sold, renovated, sold again. Mara had driven past once and seen a white wall where the entrance used to be.

She stood looking at the door until the first ferry sounded its horn.

“Want a hand?” asked Tomas, the deckhand.

“No.”

He waited.

“Yes,” she said.

They carried it into the ferry office and leaned it against the wall behind the timetable.

For the rest of the morning, Mara worked with her back to it.

At eleven, someone knocked.

Three quick taps.

She turned so sharply that her chair struck the radiator.

The blue door stood where they had left it. Beyond its edges she could see the timetable, the damp patch on the plaster, the cable leading to the electric kettle.

Again: three taps.

Her father’s knock. Impatient, even when he was arriving somewhere he had been invited.

Mara put both hands flat on the counter.

Outside, a man was arguing about whether a returned umbrella belonged to his wife. The printer needed paper. The kettle clicked off.

“Not now,” she said.

The knocking stopped.

That evening she stayed after the last crossing. She swept the floor twice. She counted the money. She cleaned a ring of tea from beneath her mug, although it had been there since November.

Then she faced the door.

She had spent twelve years becoming someone who could speak about her father without stopping midway through a sentence. She could remember his faults now, and had even begun to repeat one of his better jokes. She did not know whether she could bear to hear him tell it.

“What happens if I open it?” she asked.

Nothing answered.

“Are you actually there?”

A small sound came from the other side: a cup being set into a saucer.

Her father had drunk his tea from a saucer when it was too hot. Mara had found this disgusting at fourteen and charming at thirty, though she had never told him either thing.

She approached the door.

The brass handle was cold.

She rested her fingers on it without turning it.

“I was angry,” she said.

The harbor ropes creaked outside.

“That last day. I wasn’t busy. I could have come.”

She waited, ashamed of how readily she had offered this to a door. She had never said it to her sister, who still apologized for not calling her sooner.

Then a voice, muffled and ordinary, said, “I know.”

Mara sat on the floor.

After a while, she laughed once. Then she cried, awkwardly, with her sleeve pressed beneath her nose.

The handle did not move.

By morning the door was gone.

In its place stood a small brown teacup with a chip beside the handle.

Tomas found Mara asleep at her desk. He put his coat over her shoulders and opened the ticket window himself.

The sea returned things for another week, then stopped.

People disagreed about what it meant. The council commissioned a plaque. Someone stole it before the unveiling, which many considered appropriate.

Mara took the cup home.

Sometimes she used it. Sometimes she left it in the cupboard for months.

Once, washing it, she nearly dropped it. She caught it against the side of the sink and stood holding it tightly while the tap ran.

Then she rinsed it, dried it, and put it on the shelf with the others.
